title: 5 Reasons Your Dispensary Inventory is Inaccurate
summary: Learn why your dispensary inventory is off and how to fix it with Meadow POS
body_markdown:
A dispensary inventory discrepancy is any gap between three records that are supposed to match: what your track and trace system says you have, what your point of sale says you have, and what is physically sitting on your shelves. Keeping accurate inventory records is essential to success in[cannabis retail](https://getmeadow.com/blog/tags/cannabis-retail) , and keeping all three in sync is one of the hardest recurring jobs in the store.


When those values do not match, correcting them costs effort, time, and labor. Left unresolved, they put your business at risk of audit or fine. When[considering point-of-sale systems](https://getmeadow.com/blog/why-california-dispensaries-need-a-california-specific-pos-for-compliant) , integrating with the state's track and trace system or Metrc's API is crucial. It is just as important to understand ***how*** your POS system integrates and reports.


**This guide breaks down the five most common reasons cannabis retail inventory goes inaccurate, and the workflow fix for each one.**

## Problem #1: Selling from the Wrong Metrc Batch


Selling from the wrong Metrc batch is the most common cause of an inventory discrepancy, because the sale is real and the deduction lands on the wrong package. Your totals stay right at the store level while two individual packages quietly go wrong.


### Solution: Product Labeling and Scanning


Labeling each individual unit is the most reliable way to make sure you are selling the exact package you think you are selling. Monitor inventory transactions of packages in Meadow to follow the life cycle of any given product. To save time, use a barcode scanner to add items to an order, a cycle count, or a transfer instead of searching for the correct batch by hand.


Meadow's labeling system lets retailers create a unique label for each product in inventory, which keeps counts accurate and prevents Metrc package mix-ups.


You can also enable "scan only mode" at POS or "scan to pack" for online orders, so the correct package is the only one that can leave inventory. If that retail model does not work for your store, separate batches clearly on the retail floor and in the stockroom using Metrc tags, and give your team a written SOP for the order they should sell products in.


Read more:[Cannabis Inventory Management Tips for Your Dispensary](https://getmeadow.com/blog/7-best-practices-for-streamlining-your-dispensary-inventory-management)


[Metrc Retail ID](https://www.metrc.com/retailid/) is changing this workflow. Retail ID places a single QR code on a package at manufacturing that carries through the supply chain, so retailers can scan at point of sale without relabeling, and consumers can scan the same code to read COA and ingredient information. Adoption is furthest along in New York, where Retail ID became required for processors in November 2025 and for distributors in February 2026. In California the program remains voluntary and is growing. Metrc reported more than one million Retail ID QR codes generated in a single week across 21 markets as of mid-2025. Scanning Retail ID in Meadow is additive, not a replacement for the labels you print today.

## Problem #2: Theft


Theft shows up in your records as inventory that drops without a matching sale or adjustment, and in cannabis retail it is as often internal as external. If your store does not have a reputation for tight inventory control, loose product becomes an opportunity.


### Solution: Security and Inventory Auditing


Invest in security measures such as surveillance cameras and alarms, and train staff to actively monitor activity on the floor and in the back of house.


Read more about[How to Build a Dispensary Security Plan](https://getmeadow.com/blog/dispensary-security-plan) .


Security hardware tells you what happened. Close inventory monitoring tells you that something happened at all. Regular, frequent cycle counts account for every unit and surface patterns you would never see in a monthly reconciliation. Once you are counting often, you can address a discrepancy in a few clicks instead of a few days.

## Problem #3: Unreported Inventory Discrepancies


Damaged and returned product is the discrepancy your team creates by accident. A broken jar, a quantity adjustment, a return for an unsatisfied customer: each one is small, and each one has to be recorded the day it happens.


If your current system takes too many confusing steps to record a return in both your POS and Metrc, your staff will avoid the work. Once those skipped entries pile up, untangling them is a project.


### Solution: Make Adjustments ASAP


Build SOPs that require damaged or returned product to be reported immediately, and document those processes so they survive turnover. ## Problem #4: New Inventory Receiving Errors


Receiving errors put a discrepancy into your system before the product ever reaches the sales floor. If what arrived does not match what was invoiced and manifested, your recorded stock on hand is wrong from day one.


### Solution: Count Twice


Always count the physical inventory being delivered to your store alongside the Metrc manifest and the invoice. There are several opportunities for a mistake here. Products you did not order can arrive, quantities can be wrong, or packages can be missing from the transfer entirely. Take your time receiving deliveries and confirm every data point before you sign off.


Once you have confirmed everything is accurate, Meadow's "create purchase order from transfer" workflow does not leave packages behind, and it makes confirming inventory on hand straightforward.


Metrc can be difficult to navigate, and vendors and distributors make mistakes that leave you unsure of the next step. Meadow's support team is reachable in five minutes or less and is there to help you resolve those issues.

## Common Questions About Dispensary Inventory Discrepancies


### What counts as a significant inventory discrepancy in California?


California's Department of Cannabis Control defines a significant discrepancy as a five percent difference between a licensee's physical inventory and the inventory recorded in the track and trace system (4 CCR § 15034). When a licensee finds a significant discrepancy, the regulations require an audit and written notification to the Department. Confirm the current text of the regulation before relying on it, since the DCC updates its consolidated rules periodically.


### How often does a dispensary have to reconcile inventory?


California licensees must review the information recorded in the track and trace system at least once every 30 calendar days to confirm it matches physical inventory (4 CCR § 15051). Most operators count far more often than that. Frequent cycle counts on your highest-velocity SKUs catch a problem while it is still small enough to explain.


### Why does my POS inventory not match Metrc?


The three most common causes are a sale deducted from the wrong Metrc package, an adjustment or return recorded in one system but not the other, and a sale that failed to report during Metrc API downtime. Each one leaves your POS and Metrc telling different stories about the same product.


### What is a cycle count, and how often should I run one?


A cycle count is a physical count of a subset of your inventory, run on a rotating schedule so the whole store gets counted over time without closing for a full audit. Counting your fastest-moving categories weekly, and everything else on a rotation, keeps discrepancies from compounding between monthly reconciliations.


### Does Metrc Retail ID replace my dispensary's product labels?


No. Retail ID adds a QR code applied at manufacturing that travels with the package through the supply chain, and scanning it at point of sale is additive rather than required. Products that arrive without a Retail ID code still need a label printed at your store.
